segments.text: In April 1982, the Royal Air Force set out to drop 21 bombs on a single runway in the
Falkland Islands, and the nearest British airbase was on a volcanic island more than
6,000 km away.
The bomber itself, an aging Avro Vulcan, had nowhere near the fuel to make the round trip.
So to put that one bomber over the target, Britain launched 11 Victor Tanker aircraft
alongside it.
The tankers refueled the bomber, and they also refueled the other tankers that were going
to refuel the bomber further south, handing fuel forward in a giant relay chain across
the Atlantic until only the lone Vulcan pressed onto the island.
The longest bombing raid in history at that time was really a tanker operation with a bomber
attached to the tip.
Even on short missions today, combat jets routinely take off and head straight for a tanker 15
minutes later.
That sets up the question this video answers.
Why do modern warplanes need fuel in the sky right after leaving a runway?
And how do two metal machines flying a few meters apart at 500 kimolators an hour pump tons
of flammable jet fuel between them without colliding or catching fire?
The answer comes down to takeoff physics, two rival ways of connecting the pipe, and a hidden
web of valves and computers that keeps both aircraft balanced while their weights change
by the ton every minute.
Start with why a fighter does not simply take off with everything it needs on board.
An aircraft is at its heaviest and most sluggish the moment its wheels leave the ground.
If a strike fighter rolls down a hot runway or launches off an aircraft carrier deck carrying
both a full load of heavy bombs and full fuel tanks, it may be too heavy to climb safely at all.
The clever workaround is to take off with every weapon rack full and the fuel tanks half empty.
Once the aircraft is safely up in the thin, cold air at eight or nine kilometers altitude,
flying fast is easy, and it can sidle up to a tanker and top its tanks to the brim for the long haul to the target.
Flying up behind a giant tanker like an American KC-135, a KC-46, or a European A-330 multi-role tanker transport,
is where aerodynamics starts fighting the pilots.
A 200-ton tanker pushes a huge wave of air downward behind its wings and leaves twin tornadoes spinning off its wing tips.
As a smaller jet creeps within 10 meters of the tanker's tail, the tanker's downwash pushes the receiver's nose down,
while the receiver's own bow wave pushes upward against the tanker's tailplane.
Both autopilots and human hands have to work constantly, just to hold two aircraft motionless relative to each other
inside a box of sky a few meters wide.
Once the two aircraft are parked in that invisible box, the fuel has to cross the gap,
and militaries split into two camps over how to do it.
The first method, developed by the United States Air Force in the late 1940s and early 1950s
to feed thirsty strategic bombers, is the flying boom.
Hinged underneath the tanker's tail is a rigid telescoping metal pipe up to 15 meters long,
fitted with two small V-shaped wings near its nozzle.
In a boom refueling, the pilot of the receiving aircraft does not try to chase the pipe.
The receiver pilot simply flies into position beneath the tanker, watches a row of colored
director lights painted or lit along the tanker's belly that tell him whether to move forward,
back, up, or down, and hold steady.
Inside the tanker, a crew member called the boom operator takes over.
On older tankers, the operator lies flat on his stomach in the tail looking out a window,
while on newer ones, he sits at a console up front, wearing glasses that turn camera feeds
into a three-dimensional view.
Using a joystick, the operator literally flies the boom through the air with its little wings,
lines the nozzle up with a socket on the receiver's back, and fires an inner telescope tube forward,
to lock into the receptacle.
Because a rigid metal pipe can be wide and handle high pressure, a boom can pump roughly 3,000 to 4,000
liters of fuel a minute, filling a fighter in a couple of minutes, or a giant bomber in 15.
A rigid boom has a big limitation though.
A tanker can only carry one tail boom, so it can only feed one aircraft at a time,
and that heavy metal spar is too clumsy and dangerous to swing near the spinning rotor blades of a helicopter.
Worse, you cannot easily bolt a 15-meter rigid boom onto a small carrier-based aircraft.
That flaw produced the second method, used by the United States Navy, most other NATO air arms,
Russia and China, called probe and drogue.
Instead of a rigid pipe, the tanker reels out 20 or 30 meters of flexible steel-reinforced rubber hose
with a folding funnel-shaped basket at the end, called the drogue, which catches the wind like
a shuttlecock to hold the hose steady.
The receiving aircraft extends a steel pipe, the probe, from the side of its nose.
This time the hose has no wings and no operator steering it.
The fighter pilot has to fly his own probe straight into the middle of a tossing basket
barely 60 centimeters across.
Naval aviators dryly compare doing this in turbulence at night
to threading a needle while someone shakes the sewing machine at 500 km an hour.
If the pilot stabs too hard or off-center,
the hose can whip sideways and slap the basket straight through the fighter's canopy or rip
the probe tip off.
Even with a slower flow rate of around 1500 liters a minute, the flexible hose wins on versatility.
A large tanker can hang hose pods under both wingtips to refuel two fighters at the same time,
helicopters can plug into it safely, and a carrier fighter can carry a hose pod under its own belly to
refuel a wingman when no big tanker is within a thousand kimolators.
Whether the link is a rigid boom or a swinging basket,
the support systems inside both aircraft have to stop a disaster every second they are hooked together.
Two aircraft flying through dry air build up tens of thousands of volts of static electricity on their skins.
If fuel started flowing the instant they touched, a single spark could blow both crews out of the sky.
So the mechanical latches inside the nozzle and receptacle are wired to complete an electrical bond first,
equalizing the charge between the two airframes before a valve is allowed to crack open,
while the fuel tanks themselves are pumped full of nitrogen-rich gas
so there is not enough oxygen above the liquid to support an explosion.
At the same time, the weight of both aircraft is shifting fast.
In 5 minutes, 10 or 20 tons of liquid leaves the tanker and pours into the receiver.
If all that fuel sat in one tank, both aircraft would go tail-heavy or nose-heavy and tumble out of control.
Computers on both sides open and close manifold valves continuously during the transfers,
splitting the stream between wing, fuselage, and tail tanks to keep the center of gravity pinned in place.
And if turbulence yanks the two aircraft apart beyond a safe angle,
breakaway couplings snap the latches open and shut valves on both sides in milliseconds,
spilling barely a cupful of fuel.
Because different services kept their own connection standards for 70 years,
many modern tankers carry a tail boom and two wing hose pods at the same time,
flying into battle like a power strip stuffed with international travel adapters.
Which brings us to what people usually miss when they look at air warfare.
We judge an air force by the speed and stealth of its fighters,
and treat the converted airliners flying behind them as dull background plumbing.
My own reading is that across any vast theater like the Pacific,
the tanker is the actual center of gravity of the entire air war.
A modern fighter without a tanker has an unrefueled combat radius of roughly a thousand
kilometers, which barely gets it out to sea. That means the most decisive target for long-range
enemy missiles is not the agile stealthy fighter at the front of the formation. It is the giant
unstealthy fuel station orbiting 300 commilators behind it, because if you shoot down or chase away the
tanker, the fighters ahead of it fall into the ocean without a single shot hitting them.
So return to those 11 Victor tankers relaying a single Vulcan bomber down the length of the Atlantic
in 1982. Every part of aerial refueling, the half-empty takeoff, the winged boom, the trailing basket,
the static ground wire, and the balancing pumps, exists to erase geography from air power.
Fighter jets bring the weapons to the fight. The tanker decides whether the fight is within reach at all.
Fighter jets makes it feel comfortable.
